title: The Evil Spirit from the LORD
lead: A few stories say God sent an "evil spirit" on someone: on Abimelech and Shechem, on King Saul, and as a "lying spirit" in the mouths of Ahab's prophets. Readers since ancient times have debated whether this is a demon, an angel of judgment, or a way of describing a troubled mind (a view medieval Jewish commentators already held), and how a good God can send it.

sections.b: God sends "a harmful spirit" between Abimelech and the men of Shechem (Judges 9:23). After the LORD's Spirit leaves Saul, "an evil spirit from the LORD" terrifies him, and David's playing brings relief (1 Samuel 16:14–23); later the spirit drives Saul to throw his spear (1 Samuel 18:10–11; 1 Samuel 19:9–10). Micaiah sees a spirit volunteer to be "a lying spirit" in the mouths of Ahab's prophets (1 Kings 22:19–23). The Hebrew ra'ah can mean "evil" in the moral sense or "harmful, bad" in effect, so some translations say "harmful spirit" or "spirit of distress." Josephus and many church fathers saw a demon, others a punishing angel allowed by God. The medieval Jewish commentators Radak and Ralbag already explained Saul's spirit as melancholy, a sickness of black bile, and many modern readers likewise see the ancient way of describing what we would call depression or paranoia. Critical scholars add that early Israel traced all things, good and harmful, to God (Isaiah 45:7); later writers were less comfortable with that, as a comparison of 2 Samuel 24:1 (the LORD incites David) with 1 Chronicles 21:1 (Satan incites him) shows.
